title: Va'etchanan: don't forget what you saw (Deuteronomy 4:9)
hook: take heed lest you forget, and make it known to your children

segments.voice: Yesterday Moses pleaded, and heard rav lach. Your line was let it suffice thee. Did a no come, and did you let it be enough? Today, a warning about memory. Day four hundred eighty-eight.

Ask someone who lived through a big day where they were, and you may hear the room, the radio, the weather. Ask their grandchildren about the same day, and you may get a sentence from a textbook. Memory thins as it travels. A few generations, and a day that changed a family can become a date nobody can quite place. Moses is speaking to people who were children at Sinai, or not yet born, and he seems to know how this goes. So he stops in the middle of his speech and gives them a warning.
screen: `THE ROOM, THE RADIO, THE WEATHER.` → `A LINE FROM A TEXTBOOK.` → `MOSES STOPS TO WARN THEM.`

segments.voice: The warning, in the old Jewish translation, begins: "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget." Forget what? The things your eyes saw. He means Sinai: the day you stood before God at Horeb, the mountain burning, the voice out of the fire. And the verse goes on: don't let them slip from your heart all the days of your life, but make them known to your children and your children's children. Notice the order. First, guard yourself. Take heed. In Hebrew, hishamer lecha, watch yourself, be on guard. Memory isn't automatic; it's something you protect, like a flame in wind. Then, pass it on. Not as a lecture. As testimony: what your eyes saw. The medieval teacher Nachmanides, called the Ramban, read this verse as a full commandment, to never let the experience of Sinai leave your mind, and to tell it to every generation. And there's a curious afterlife to the words keep thy soul diligently. Later teachers heard in them a duty to look after your own body and life too, so the verse about memory became a verse about health. Both readings meet in the same place. What you were given has to be guarded, or it's gone. Moses can't make his listeners' grandchildren remember Sinai. He can only make sure his listeners don't forget, and tell it.
screen: `TAKE HEED, LEST THOU FORGET.` · `THE THINGS YOUR EYES SAW.` · `TO YOUR CHILDREN'S CHILDREN.` · `GUARD IT, OR IT'S GONE.` · then, large: `DON'T FORGET WHAT YOU SAW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write down one memory. Settle, and breathe. Let one moment come back that you never want to lose. A birth, a goodbye, a kindness, a moment when something felt holy, or just true. Don't explain it yet. See it. Where were you standing? What did you hear? Who was there? When the sit is over, write it down in a few plain sentences, the way your eyes saw it, so someone younger could read it one day. The bell holds the time.
Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. The portion where Moses, after his own no, turns to guarding what his people saw.
Your line: don't forget what you saw. Today, tell one memory to someone younger, the way you actually saw it. Day four hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Jewish prayer books include a short list of things to remember daily, and the day of Sinai, drawn from Deuteronomy 4:9–10, is one of them; Nachmanides counts not forgetting Sinai as a commandment.

fork.setup: you lived through something your grandchildren will only read about. what does the verse ask?
options: let the history books tell it.
guard it in yourself, then tell it to them.
fork.reveal: take heed to thyself lest thou forget, then make it known to your children and your children's children.

original.note: Hebrew: take heed to thyself, guard yourself. the opening of Moses' warning against forgetting.

trapdoor: what you thought: a reminder to remember the past.
what it means: memory has to be guarded like a flame, then handed on as testimony, what your own eyes saw.
what a scholar hears: the Ramban counts not forgetting Sinai as a commandment; keep thy soul was also read as guarding your health.

sources.quoted: Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget

sources.ref: Nachmanides, glosses on Maimonides' Sefer HaMitzvot (negative commandments he adds, 2)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): softened the hook's 'anyone over seventy' generalization and the superlative 'the most important thing'; 'many prayer books' softened to 'some'.

Deuteronomy 4:9 opening quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; the rest of the verse ('the things which thine eyes saw', 'make them known unto thy children and thy children's children') paraphrased; verify.
Ramban counts not forgetting the Sinai experience among the negative commandments he adds to Maimonides' list; confirm the numbering.

The health reading of 'keep thy soul diligently' is popular and traces to the story in Berakhot 32b, which cites Deuteronomy 4:9 and 4:15; Keeper may want to note that halachic sources usually cite 4:15.
The 'remembrances' recited after morning prayers (the six remembrances) include standing at Sinai; custom varies.
